Why would a children's heart surgeon ask Ferrari for help?
Great Ormond Street Hospital, London.
A baby has just survived heart surgery.
But the danger isn't over.
Next, the move to intensive care.
Every tube, wire and monitor gets unplugged, moved, and plugged back in.
Several teams crowd one tiny bed, and details get missed.
Heart surgeon Martin Elliott and intensive care chief Allan Goldman looked to Formula One.
A pit stop: twenty mechanics, one car, done in seconds, and nobody gets in anyone's way.
So they went to Ferrari, in Maranello.
Ferrari's team studied videos of the hospital's handovers.
The fix came straight from the pit lane.
One leader runs the handover, the anaesthetist, just like the lollipop man.
Everyone gets one job, in a fixed order.
A checklist makes sure nothing is forgotten.
They borrowed ideas from airline pilots too.
The result? Across about fifty handovers, technical errors dropped by forty-two percent.
Missing information was almost cut in half.
A sport chasing tenths of a second taught doctors to protect what matters most.
So next time someone asks you...
